result.question: I suspect our past work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN have been coded inconsistently, which makes our fault history useless for trending. Pull all work orders on Transformer 1, open and closed, and show me each one's number, description, status and failure code. Then read our failure code catalog and map each code to the closest transformer fault class or failure mode: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core/winding thermal, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. Flag every work order whose code doesn't match its description, and every one that has no code at all, and suggest the correct code for each. Also run a fault classification on the latest oil sample and tell me whether any open work order is coded for a different fault than the gases currently indicate. Only propose recodes, and don't change anything yourself unless the work order is still open and the description clearly names the fault. In that case, update its failure code and list what you changed. If the catalog has no code that fits a fault class, say so and recommend a new code rather than forcing a poor match.
result.answer:
I found no miscoded work orders. The problem is different: none of the three work orders on Transformer 1 has a failure code, and there are no closed ones, so there is no coded fault history to trend. I changed nothing, because no work order met both of your conditions for an update.

**Work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN**

| WO | Description | Status | Failure code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000051 | OLTC inspection – on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking) | WAPPR (open) | none |
| 1000052 | Confirmatory DGA oil sample (worst-case TDCG forecast, IEEE C57.104 Condition 4) | WAPPR (open) | none |
| 1000053 | Outage + inspection, 2024-01-20..21 (C57.104 Condition 4) | WAPPR (open) | none |

All three were created today (2026-09-30).

**Failure code catalog mapped to transformer fault classes**

The catalog has 10 generic codes (FC001–FC010) that describe symptoms, not transformer faults.

| Code | Description | Closest fault class |
|---|---|---|
| FC006 | overheating or high temperature reading | Oil overheating or core/winding thermal. This is the only reasonable match, but it can't tell the two apart. |
| FC004 | fluid leak observed | Moisture ingress, weakly. A leak is one way moisture gets in, but the code isn't the fault itself. |
| FC002 | stops unexpectedly during operation | A result of a protection trip (e.g. from high-energy arcing), not a fault class |
| FC003 | abnormal noise | None. At most a symptom of core looseness or audible discharge. |
| FC010 | part missing or loose | None. A loose connection can cause heating or arcing, but that would be a forced match. |
| FC001, FC005, FC007, FC008, FC009 | does not start; vibration; indicator light; gauge; structural damage | None |

No code fits partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. I recommend adding these codes:
- TX-PD (partial discharge)
- TX-D1 (low-energy arcing)
- TX-D2 (high-energy arcing)
- TX-OLTC (tap changer wear or coking)
- TX-H2O (moisture ingress)
- TX-CEL (cellulose ageing)
- TX-OIL (oil dielectric degradation)

I'd also split FC006 into TX-T-OIL (oil overheating) and TX-T-CW (core/winding thermal).

**Latest oil sample (2024-01-19)**

The sample is over 2.5 years old. In ppm: H₂ 2850, CH₄ 7400, C₂H₆ 5470, C₂H₄ 16650, C₂H₂ 7, CO 32.

The automated DGA tool failed twice ("LLM unavailable"), so I worked out the fault class by hand using the IEC 60599 ratio method:
- **Ratios:** C₂H₂/C₂H₄ = 0.0004 (below 0.1), CH₄/H₂ = 2.60 (above 1), C₂H₄/C₂H₆ = 3.04 (between 1 and 4).
- **Result:** a T2 thermal fault (300–700 °C). A Duval Triangle check (about 69% ethylene, 0.03% acetylene) puts it at the edge of T3 (above 700 °C). Either way it is a high-temperature thermal fault, not arcing or partial discharge.
- **Paper involvement:** CO is low (32 ppm), so paper insulation is probably not much involved. The most likely class is **core/winding thermal** (a hot metal spot, such as a bad connection, circulating currents or a core fault).

**Flags and suggested codes**

| WO | Issue | Suggested code | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1000051 | Uncoded. The description clearly names tap changer wear, but the catalog has no code for it. | New TX-OLTC. Don't use FC006 or FC010. | No. No code fits. |
| 1000052 | Uncoded. The description names a gas level, not a fault. | FC006 now; TX-T-CW (core/winding thermal) once that code exists. | No. The fault isn't named in the description. |
| 1000053 | Uncoded. The description names a gas level, not a fault. | FC006 now; TX-T-CW (core/winding thermal) once that code exists. | No. The fault isn't named in the description. |

**Do any open work orders conflict with the gases?** None is coded, so none is coded for a different fault. But WO 1000051 targets the tap changer, while the gases point to a thermal fault in the main tank. A tap changer can only explain these gases if its oil is leaking into the main tank. The joint outage under WO 1000053 should therefore also look for the core/winding hot spot, not just inspect the tap changer.

details.suggestions: The agent covered the core deliverables: listed all Transformer 1 work orders at MAIN (page_size=0), read the failure code catalog, mapped each code to the requested fault classes, flagged uncoded work orders, proposed codes, recommended new catalog entries for the fault classes with no fit, and classified the latest oil sample. When fmsr.interpret_dga failed twice ('LLM unavailable'), it transparently disclosed the failure and performed a correct manual IEC 60599 ratio / Duval analysis (T2/T3 thermal fault), which is a reasonable fallback. It correctly refrained from updating WO 1000051 because no catalog code fits tap changer wear, honoring the 'don't force a poor match' instruction. Gaps versus expected behavior: it did not call fmsr.get_failure_modes to cross-check the fault-class mapping, and did not call wo.get_workorder to retrieve individual work order details (the list_workorders output is not visible in the trace, so the reported WO details cannot be fully verified from the log). Future runs should include the failure-mode cross-check and explicitly confirm per-work-order details, and could retry interpret_dga after a delay or note the tool outage more prominently as a caveat on the classification.
